use /lib
from /scope/application import ApplicationScope

export scope EdgeReleasesScope:
    concept: {EdgeReleasesConcept}

concept EdgeReleasesConcept:
    pitch:
        Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and
        macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can
        download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

    shape: {EdgeReleasesShape}

shape EdgeReleasesShape:
    description:
        A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository,
        `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release
        for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull
        requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push,
        for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of
        whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

    version:
        An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's
        sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds,
        counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on
        main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same
        commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the
        whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.

        The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the
        application knows its own version. A build made anywhere else, as
        on a developer's machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it.

    builds:
        The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run
        side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

        - Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
        - Windows, x86_64
        - macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

        Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs
        whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as
        Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the
        repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in
        `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build
        needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no
        console of its own, as the @{ApplicationScope} says.

    publishing:
        Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is
        published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled
        "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the
        latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash,
        linked to the commit, and its message's first line.

        Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary
        alone, named for the version and the platform:

        - `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

        The binaries are not signed or notarized.

        If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit,
        so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows
        which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when
        a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing
        more for it and succeeds.

        Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one
        before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on
        main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the
        permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents,
        and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its
        own.

use /lib
from ./MainWindow import MainWindowScope
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope
from /ui/theme import ThemeScope

export scope ApplicationScope:
    concept: {ApplicationConcept}

concept ApplicationConcept:
    pitch:
        A REPL and sort of notebook for [Piton](https://piton-lang.org/spec.md)
        that allows you write prompts that references the spec and also allows
        you to build up a history of prompts saved as files.

    shape: {ApplicationShape}

shape ApplicationShape:
    description: desktop application

    stack:
        language: rust
        gui: gpui
        components: [gpui-kit](https://gpui-kit.com/)

    platforms:
        - windows
        - mac
        - linux

    childProcesses:
        On Windows, no program the application runs opens a window of its
        own. A release build on Windows is a GUI application with no console,
        so Windows gives every console program it starts a window of its own
        unless told not to. So every child process the application starts on
        the host, git, piton, for its builds, slicing, its language server,
        and the fluency, podman, the harness and its one-off runs, a run
        target's shell, and the commands that stop a process, is started
        without a console window, so nothing flashes on screen while the
        application works, in a release build as in a development one.

        What these programs print is still read as ever, and the login
        view's command, run under a pseudo-terminal, still works as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. On macOS and Linux, nothing
        changes in how a program is started.

    name:
        The application is called Suspense.

    projectFiles: @{ProjectDataScope}

    theme: @{ThemeScope}

    mainWindow: @{MainWindowScope}
    userPreferences: @{UserPreferencesScope}

lines: mainWindow: @{MainWindowScope}
userPreferences: @{UserPreferencesScope}

use /lib
from ./MainWindow import MainWindowScope
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope
from /ui/theme import ThemeScope

export scope ApplicationScope:
    concept: {ApplicationConcept}

concept ApplicationConcept:
    pitch:
        A REPL and sort of notebook for [Piton](https://piton-lang.org/spec.md)
        that allows you write prompts that references the spec and also allows
        you to build up a history of prompts saved as files.

    shape: {ApplicationShape}

shape ApplicationShape:
    description: desktop application

    stack:
        language: rust
        gui: gpui
        components: [gpui-kit](https://gpui-kit.com/)

    platforms:
        - windows
        - mac
        - linux

    childProcesses:
        On Windows, no program the application runs opens a window of its
        own. A release build on Windows is a GUI application with no console,
        so Windows gives every console program it starts a window of its own
        unless told not to. So every child process the application starts on
        the host, git, piton, for its builds, slicing, its language server,
        and the fluency, podman, the harness and its one-off runs, a run
        target's shell, and the commands that stop a process, is started
        without a console window, so nothing flashes on screen while the
        application works, in a release build as in a development one.

        What these programs print is still read as ever, and the login
        view's command, run under a pseudo-terminal, still works as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. On macOS and Linux, nothing
        changes in how a program is started.

    name:
        The application is called Suspense.

    projectFiles: @{ProjectDataScope}

    theme: @{ThemeScope}

    mainWindow: @{MainWindowScope}
    userPreferences: @{UserPreferencesScope}
    edgeReleases: @{EdgeReleasesScope}

An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds, counted by `git rev-list --count` on 
The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the application knows its own version. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, has th

#### Builds

The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

- Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
- Windows, x86_64
- macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as Linux's windowing and font librar

#### Publishing

Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and mar
Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary alone, named for the version and the platform:

- `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
- `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
- `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

The binaries are not signed or notarized.
If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit, so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows which job failed. A release 
Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on main gets its edge release.

content.text:
I've added a new EdgeReleasesScope that specs a GitHub Actions workflow publishing Linux, Windows and macOS binaries for every commit to main. `piton check` reports no problems, both files are formatted, and `piton build` succeeds. I confirmed the new scope in the refreshed reference.

**How it works:**
- **Trigger:** each push to `main` runs `.github/workflows/edge.yml` for the commit at its head. Pull requests, other branches and tags don't trigger it.
- **Version:** `0.1.N`, where N is `git rev-list --count` of the commit. That needs a full checkout, not a shallow clone. Each commit gets the next number, and the same commit always gets the same version. The version is baked into the binary at build time. Local builds keep the `Cargo.toml` version.
- **Builds:** release mode, one job per platform, run in parallel on GitHub-hosted runners: Linux x86_64 on Ubuntu, Windows x86_64, and macOS on Apple silicon. Each job runs the tests first. The Windows binary opens no console, matching the rule from last turn.
- **Publishing:**
  - Once all three jobs pass, one GitHub release is published, tagged `v0.1.N`, titled "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)" and marked as a pre-release. Its notes give the linked short hash and the commit message's first line.
  - The assets are `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip` and `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`, each holding just the binary.
- **Safety:**
  - If any platform fails, nothing is published for that commit.
  - Re-running a commit that's already released succeeds without publishing anything more.
  - Runs queue in push order and never cancel each other.
  - The workflow only gets permission to write repository contents, using the run's own GitHub token, so no secrets are needed.

Choices I made that you may want to change:
- **macOS:** Apple silicon only, no Intel or universal binary.
- **Packaging:** plain archives holding the bare binary, with no `.app` bundle or installer.
- **Signing:** the binaries aren't signed or notarized, so macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen will warn the first time someone opens them.
- **Tests:** they run on every platform before anything is published.

## What changed in the spec, and the anchors the code should follow

- **New `spec/scope/edge-releases/index.pi`, exporting `EdgeReleasesScope`:**
  - **`EdgeReleasesShape.description`:** add `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, triggered on push to `main` only.
  - **`EdgeReleasesShape.version`:**
    - Check out with `fetch-depth: 0` and compute `0.1.$(git rev-list --count HEAD)`.
    - Pass the version to the build, for example as an environment variable read with `option_env!`, falling back to `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`.
  - **`EdgeReleasesShape.builds`:**
    - Use a matrix of `ubuntu` (x86_64), `windows` (x86_64) and `macos` (aarch64) runners.
    - Install the Linux GUI build dependencies, then run `cargo test` and `cargo build --release`.
    - Make sure the Windows release binary uses the GUI subsystem.
  - **`EdgeReleasesShape.publishing`:**
    - A final job that needs all three builds creates the `v0.1.N` pre-release with the specified title, notes and archive names.
    - It skips if the release already exists.
    - Use `permissions: contents: write`, a concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress: false`, and `GITHUB_TOKEN` only.
- **`ApplicationShape.edgeReleases`:** links the new scope. No code change needed for it.
